reference.source: Diving and hyperbaric medicine / otolaryngology references
clinicalPearls: The commonest injury in divers and a frequent problem in air travellers, caused by failure to equalise middle ear pressure during descent
Inability to open the Eustachian tube, often from upper respiratory congestion, prevents pressure equalisation
Features range from ear fullness and pain to tympanic membrane haemorrhage, effusion and, in severe cases, rupture
Conductive hearing loss and vertigo may occur, and forceful equalisation can cause inner ear barotrauma
Otoscopy grades the injury from mild retraction and erythema to frank haemorrhage or perforation
Prevention centres on gentle equalisation techniques and avoiding diving or flying with nasal congestion
reference.pathophysiology: During descent the ambient pressure rises and, unless the middle ear is equalised through the Eustachian tube, the relative negative pressure in the middle ear draws the tympanic membrane inward and engorges and ruptures mucosal vessels, producing effusion and haemorrhage. If the tube cannot be actively opened, the pressure differential increases until tissue injury or membrane rupture occurs. Forceful attempts at equalisation against a blocked tube can transmit pressure to the inner ear and cause more serious inner ear barotrauma.
additionalDifferentials: Inner ear barotrauma or perilymph fistula
Decompression sickness affecting the vestibular system
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy to grade the tympanic membrane injury
Audiometry and tympanometry if hearing loss or effusion is present
Assessment for inner ear involvement if vertigo or sensorineural loss occurs
Evaluation of Eustachian tube function and nasal pathology
Consideration of a diving-medicine review before return to diving
redFlags: Sensorineural hearing loss or persistent vertigo suggesting inner ear barotrauma
reference.prognosis: Most cases resolve over days to weeks with conservative care; perforations often heal spontaneously, but inner ear barotrauma can cause permanent hearing loss.
pitfalls: Missing coexisting inner ear barotrauma when there is vertigo or sensorineural loss
Advising continued diving or flying with nasal congestion
Confusing it with acute otitis media
references: Diving and hyperbaric medicine references (standard reference)
